Eucalyptus globulus subsp. maidenii, commonly known as Maiden's gum, is a subspecies of tree that is endemic to southeastern Australia. It has mostly smooth bark with some persistent slabs of old bark at the base, juvenile leaves with one glaucous side, lance-shaped adult leaves, flower buds arranged in groups of seven, white flowers and conical, pedicellate, sometimes glaucous fruit that is more or less square in cross-section- Eucalyptus globulus subsp. maidenii. Australian Plant Census.
- Eucalyptus globulus subsp. maidenii. Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research.

## Description

Eucalyptus globulus subsp. maidenii is a tree that typically grows to a height of and forms a lignotuber. The fruit is a woody, conical, sometimes glaucous capsule, long and wide with the valves at about rim level.

- M. Ian H. Brooker, Andrew V. Slee. Eucalyptus globulus subsp. maidenii. Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria.
- George M. Chippendale. Eucalyptus globulus subsp. maidenii. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra.

## Taxonomy and naming

Maiden's gum was first formally described in 1890 by Ferdinand von Mueller who gave it the name Eucalyptus maidenii and published the description in Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales from collections by William Bäuerlen. In 1974, James Barrie Kirkpatrick described four subspecies of E. globulus and changed the name E. maidenii to E. globulus subsp. maidenii. The epithet maidenii honours Joseph Maiden.

- Eucalyptus maidenii. APNI.
- Ferdinand von Mueller. Notes on a new species of Eucalyptus (Eucalyptus maidenii) from southern New South Wales. Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales. 1890.
- James Barrie Kirkpatrick. The numerical intraspecific taxonomy of Eucalyptus globulus Labill. (Myrtaceae). The Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society. September 1974.
- Eucalyptus globulus subsp. maidenii. APNI.

## Distribution and habitat

This subspecies of E. globulus grows in forest in mountain valleys, on slopes and ridges in near-coastal ranges of New South Wales south of the Shoalhaven River and in eastern Victoria near the upper reaches of the Genoa and Cann Rivers.

- Ken Hill. Eucalyptus maidenii. Royal Botanic Garden Sydney.

BRIEF DESCRIPTION A tall tree reaching up to 35-45 m or even 75 m in height, while the trunk may reach a diameter of up to 250 cm. Usually the tree has a good form with a straight bole up to 2/3 of the tree height. Heartwood light brown, with close uniform texture, grains sometimes interlocked, hard and moderately strong and durable. USES The wood is used for general construction purposes. GROWING PERIOD Perennial. Withstands droughts of up to 3 months. COMMON NAMES Maiden's gum. FURTHER INF Scientific synonym: E. maidenii. It can in tropical and subtropical regions be found at elevations between 200-1000 m. The natural latitudinal range in Australia is 35-37.5°S. The tree thrives in moist, sheltered mountain valleys, but can also be found on ridges and mountain slopes. Mentioned as a possible agroforestry species. Yields may be between 5-50 m3/ha/year.

# Eucalyptus globulus subsp. maidenii

## Maiden's gum

Classification

Eucalyptus | Symphyomyrtus | Maidenaria | Euryotae | Globulares | Euglobulares

Nomenclature

Eucalyptus globulus subsp. maidenii (F.Muell.) J.B.Kirkp., J. Linn. Soc., Bot. 69: 101 (1975).
Eucalyptus maidenii F.Muell., Proc. Linn. Soc. New South Wales ser. 2, 4: 1020 (1890). T: Colombo, NSW, June 1887, W.Bäuerlen s.n.; lecto: NSW, fide J.H.Maiden, Crit. Revis. Eucalyptus 2: 265 (1913); isolecto: MEL.

Description

Tree to 50 m tall. Forming a lignotuber.
Bark smooth apart from base which has persistent slabs, shedding in large strips and slabs; smooth bark white, cream, grey, pink, yellowish or pale creamy orange, often with ribbons of decorticated bark in the upper branches; branchlets occasionally glaucous.
Juvenile growth (coppice or field seedlings to 50 cm): stem square in cross-section and prominently winged, glaucous; juvenile leaves opposite and sessile for many pairs, elliptical to oblong then ovate to lanceolate or falcate, 4–11 cm long, 1.7–6 cm wide, base amplexicaul, margin sometimes crenulate, usually discolorous with upper surface green or slightly glaucous and the lower surface copiously white-waxy.
